questions.q: A 35-year-old male presents with painless ulcer on the glans penis for 2 weeks. The base is clean and indurated. Dark-field microscopy reveals corkscrew-shaped motile organisms. What is the most appropriate treatment?
opts: Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU single IM injection
Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days
questions.exp: Primary syphilis (Treponema pallidum). Benzathine penicillin G 2.4 MU IM single dose is the treatment of choice for primary syphilis per WHO and NACO guidelines. Doxycycline is an alternative for penicillin-allergic patients.

questions.q: A 28-year-old HIV-positive woman develops widespread vesicles on an erythematous base over her chest and back, crossing dermatomal boundaries. She has fever and lymphadenopathy. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Disseminated herpes zoster occurs when VZV reactivates and spreads beyond the primary dermatome, especially in immunocompromised individuals (CD4 < 200). Crossing dermatomal boundaries and visceral involvement are hallmarks.

questions.q: A 22-year-old presents with hypopigmented, anaesthetic patches on the trunk with thickened peripheral nerves. Slit-skin smear shows 3+ AFB. Which type of leprosy does he have?
questions.exp: BL leprosy has numerous lesions (more than BT), positive smear (BI 3+–5+), and nerve thickening. Tuberculoid leprosy has negative smear. Lepromatous has BI of 4+–6+ with diffuse infiltration. The clinical picture of a few hypopigmented patches with BI 3+ fits BL leprosy.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with tense blisters on normal-appearing and erythematous skin, predominantly on the flexural areas. Nikolsky's sign is negative. Biopsy shows subepidermal blister with eosinophils. DIF shows linear IgG and C3 at the BMZ. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Bullous pemphigoid: tense subepidermal blisters, negative Nikolsky's, linear IgG+C3 at BMZ (targets BP180/BP230), flexural predilection, eosinophil-rich infiltrate. DH has granular IgA deposits. EBA also linear IgG but at the floor of the blister on salt-split skin.

questions.q: A 30-year-old male presents with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base over the elbow and knee with intense pruritus. Biopsy shows neutrophils at the dermal papilla tips. IgA deposits are found in a granular pattern at the DEJ. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.exp: Dermatitis herpetiformis is associated with gluten-sensitive enteropathy. Granular IgA at DEJ is pathognomonic. Dapsone provides rapid symptomatic relief, but gluten-free diet is the definitive treatment.

questions.q: A 40-year-old woman on methotrexate for psoriasis develops nausea, oral ulcers, and pancytopenia. Which drug should be immediately given?
questions.exp: Methotrexate toxicity (mucositis, bone marrow suppression) is treated with folinic acid (leucovorin rescue), which bypasses the DHFR blockade. Folic acid supplementation is used prophylactically but cannot rescue acute toxicity.

questions.q: A 50-year-old male presents with a shiny, pearly papule with rolled borders and telangiectasia on the nose, present for 6 months. What is the most common subtype and the treatment of choice?
opts: Squamous cell carcinoma; wide local excision
Basal cell carcinoma, nodular type; Mohs micrographic surgery
Melanoma; wide excision with 2 cm margin
questions.exp: Nodular BCC is the most common subtype of BCC, which is the most common skin cancer. Mohs surgery has the highest cure rate (>99%) for facial BCC. Rolled (pearly) borders with telangiectasia are classic.

questions.q: A 25-year-old presents with ring-shaped scaly lesion on the scalp with broken hair stubs and cervical lymphadenopathy. KOH shows endothrix spores. What is the most appropriate treatment?
questions.exp: Tinea capitis with endothrix pattern (e.g., Trichophyton tonsurans) requires systemic antifungals. Griseofulvin remains first-line in India, especially in children. Topical agents are inadequate for scalp dermatophytosis due to the follicular involvement.

questions.q: A 32-year-old female develops malar rash after sun exposure, oral ulcers, alopecia, and arthralgia. Anti-dsDNA antibody is positive. Which complement pathway is most commonly activated?
questions.exp: In SLE, immune complexes (anti-dsDNA + DNA) activate the classical complement pathway (C1q, C4, C2). Low C3 and C4 indicate consumption. The classical pathway is the primary mechanism in lupus nephritis and other manifestations.

questions.q: A 60-year-old farmer presents with a dark, warty plaque on his hand after a thorn prick 3 years ago. Biopsy shows copper-penny bodies (Medlar bodies). What is the causative organism?
questions.exp: Chromoblastomycosis (chromomycosis) is caused by dematiaceous fungi like Fonsecaea pedrosoi (most common), Cladophialophora carrionii, and Phialophora verrucosa. Medlar bodies (sclerotic cells) are the pathognomonic finding on histology.

questions.q: A 28-year-old male presents with multiple grouped papulovesicles on the genitals. PCR confirms HSV-2. He has had 6 recurrences in the last year. What is the most appropriate management?
opts: Acyclovir 400 mg TDS for 5 days at each recurrence
Valacyclovir 2 g BD for 1 day at each recurrence
No treatment required; lesions are self-limiting
questions.exp: With 6+ recurrences per year, suppressive therapy with acyclovir 400 mg BD (or valacyclovir 500 mg OD) is recommended to reduce frequency and transmission risk. Episodic treatment is used for fewer recurrences.

questions.q: A 45-year-old presents with well-defined erythematous plaques with silvery scales on the elbows and knees. Which histological feature is most specific for psoriasis?
opts: Regular acanthosis with suprapapillary thinning and Munro microabscesses
questions.exp: Psoriasis histology: regular acanthosis, parakeratosis, absent granular layer, dilated capillaries in elongated dermal papillae, suprapapillary thinning, and Munro microabscesses (neutrophils in stratum corneum) / Kogoj spongiform pustules.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child presents with honey-coloured crusted lesions around the mouth and nose that began as thin-walled vesicles. Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters. What is the most likely causative organism?
questions.exp: Bullous impetigo is predominantly caused by Staphylococcus aureus (phage group II, types 55/71) producing exfoliative toxin A. Non-bullous impetigo may be caused by S. aureus or S. pyogenes. Honey-coloured crust is classic for non-bullous, but thin-walled blisters suggest bullous impetigo from S. aureus.

questions.q: A 55-year-old diabetic presents with rapidly spreading painful skin necrosis with gas formation in the subcutaneous tissue. Crepitus is felt on palpation. What is the first-line management?
opts: Urgent surgical debridement with broad-spectrum antibiotics
questions.exp: Necrotizing fasciitis is a surgical emergency. Prompt radical debridement is life-saving and cannot be delayed for any reason. Broad-spectrum antibiotics (covering polymicrobial organisms) are adjunctive. Delay in surgery is the main determinant of mortality.

questions.q: A patient with Type 1 lepra reaction presents with sudden onset of painful erythematous swelling of previously quiescent lesions and acute neuritis of the ulnar nerve. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.exp: Type 1 (reversal) reaction involves cell-mediated immune response and acute neuritis. Oral corticosteroids are the treatment of choice to prevent permanent nerve damage. Thalidomide is used for Type 2 (ENL) reactions, not Type 1.

questions.q: A 20-year-old female presents with multiple comedones, papules, and pustules on the face. She wants to start isotretinoin. Which mandatory baseline investigation is essential before initiating treatment?
questions.exp: Isotretinoin is a potent teratogen (Category X). Pregnancy test (urine/serum β-hCG) is mandatory before initiating and monitoring during treatment. Lipid profile (triglycerides, cholesterol) is also essential due to hypertriglyceridemia risk. iPLEDGE enrollment is required in many countries.

questions.q: A 38-year-old male presents with scaly hypopigmented patches on the chest and back that fluoresce golden-yellow under Wood's lamp. KOH shows short hyphae and spherical spores ('spaghetti and meatballs'). What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Tinea versicolor caused by Malassezia furfur/globosa shows the classic 'spaghetti and meatballs' pattern (short hyphae + budding yeast) on KOH. Golden-yellow fluorescence under Wood's lamp is characteristic. Hypopigmentation results from azelaic acid inhibiting melanogenesis.

questions.q: A 70-year-old man presents with a rapidly growing, well-differentiated keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma on sun-damaged skin that developed within 6 weeks. It has a central keratin-filled crater with rolled edges. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Keratoacanthoma is characterized by rapid growth over 4–8 weeks, a central keratin-filled crater, and spontaneous involution over months. While some classify it as a variant of SCC, its rapid onset and crateriform morphology distinguish it clinically. Excision is recommended.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with symmetric sclerosis of skin, Raynaud's phenomenon, dysphagia, and pulmonary fibrosis. Anti-Scl-70 antibody is positive. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Anti-Scl-70 (anti-topoisomerase I) is associated with diffuse cutaneous SSc. It correlates with pulmonary fibrosis and worse prognosis. Anti-centromere antibody is associated with limited cutaneous SSc (CREST syndrome).

questions.q: A 4-year-old child presents with diffuse erythema and superficial skin peeling after fever. The skin separates with gentle lateral pressure (Nikolsky's sign positive). Blood culture grows Staphylococcus aureus phage group II. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: SSSS is caused by exfoliative toxins A and B from S. aureus phage group II. It predominantly affects children under 5. Cleavage is intraepidermal (granular layer) unlike TEN which is subepidermal. Nikolsky's sign is positive. Skin biopsy differentiates from TEN.

questions.q: A 26-year-old woman with lichen planus has wickham's striae on buccal mucosa. Which immunological mechanism is responsible?
opts: Type IV hypersensitivity (cell-mediated, CD8+ T cells targeting basal keratinocytes)
questions.exp: Lichen planus involves cytotoxic CD8+ T lymphocytes attacking basal keratinocytes (apoptosis), mediated by Type IV hypersensitivity. DIF shows shaggy fibrinogen deposits at the BMZ and colloid bodies (cytoid bodies). Wickham's striae are due to focal hypergranulosis.

questions.q: A 32-year-old male presents with non-tender, painless, firm papules and nodules on the distal parts of fingers and dorsum of hands. He has joint pain and elevated ESR. Biopsy shows palisading granuloma with central fibrinoid necrosis. What is the diagnosis?
questions.exp: Rheumatoid nodules occur over bony prominences (olecranon, fingers) in seropositive RA patients. Histology shows palisading granuloma with central fibrinoid necrosis. Granuloma annulare shows incomplete palisading without necrobiosis; necrobiosis lipoidica occurs on pretibial areas in diabetics.

questions.q: A patient undergoes a patch test. After 48 hours, the result shows erythema, papules, and vesicles at the test site. What type of hypersensitivity reaction is this?
questions.exp: Patch testing detects Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity, i.e., allergic contact dermatitis. The reaction peaks at 48–96 hours and is mediated by sensitized CD4+ T (Th1) cells. Type I reactions occur within minutes.

questions.q: A 29-year-old male presents with warty, cauliflower-like lesion on the corona of penis for 8 months. HPV typing reveals HPV 6 and 11. What is the treatment of choice?
questions.exp: Condylomata acuminata (genital warts) caused by HPV 6 and 11 (low risk). For keratinized, large lesions, patient-applied imiquimod (immune response modifier) or podophyllotoxin (patient-applied) are first-line. Physician-applied podophyllin is an option but imiquimod has fewer side effects and higher clearance rates.

questions.q: A 55-year-old male with psoriasis develops painful joint swelling affecting the distal interphalangeal joints, with nail pitting and onycholysis. Rheumatoid factor is negative. What is the characteristic radiological finding?
questions.exp: Psoriatic arthritis (DIP involvement, seronegative) shows 'pencil-in-cup' deformity on X-ray due to bone resorption at phalangeal tips and adjacent joint cup formation. Bamboo spine is seen in ankylosing spondylitis; juxta-articular osteoporosis is a feature of RA.

questions.q: A 22-year-old presents with recurrent painful aphthous ulcers, uveitis, and scrotal ulceration. What is the investigation of choice?
questions.exp: Behcet's disease is characterized by recurrent oral and genital ulcers, ocular involvement (uveitis), and skin manifestations. The pathergy test (positive if papule/pustule develops at a needle-prick site after 24–48 hours) is a specific though not sensitive diagnostic test. HLA-B51 is associated but not diagnostic.

questions.q: While performing dermoscopy on a melanocytic lesion, you find an atypical pigment network, irregular dots/globules, regression structures, and blue-white veil. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Dermoscopic criteria for melanoma include atypical pigment network, irregular streaks, atypical dots/globules, regression structures (white scar-like areas), and blue-white veil. The 7-point checklist and ABCD rule are used for diagnosis.

questions.q: A patient with widespread plaque psoriasis fails to respond to methotrexate. He is started on adalimumab. What is the mechanism of action of this drug?
opts: Fully human monoclonal antibody against TNF-alpha
questions.exp: Adalimumab is a fully human monoclonal antibody targeting TNF-alpha, approved for moderate-to-severe plaque psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis. Secukinumab/ixekizumab target IL-17A; abatacept blocks CD28 co-stimulation; ustekinumab targets p40 (IL-12/23).

questions.q: A 40-year-old male presents with a well-defined depigmented patch on the right wrist for 2 years. The hairs within the patch are also white. Wood's lamp examination shows bright white fluorescence. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.exp: Vitiligo shows accentuation under Wood's lamp (bright chalky white fluorescence) due to complete loss of melanocytes. Leukotrichia (white hairs) indicates melanocyte destruction in follicular reservoir—a poor prognostic sign for repigmentation. Post-inflammatory hypopigmentation does not fluoresce brightly.

questions.q: A 52-year-old male with chronic alcoholism presents with pellagra. Which vitamin deficiency is responsible?
questions.exp: Pellagra is caused by niacin (Vitamin B3 / nicotinic acid) deficiency, often precipitated by a corn-based diet low in tryptophan, alcoholism, or carcinoid syndrome. The classic triad is Dermatitis, Diarrhea, and Dementia (3 Ds). The rash is photodistributed with Casal's necklace on the neck.
